extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York; readers debating the proposed U.S. Constitution and federal vs. state powers
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria and interpretive rules for assessing the proper scope, limits, and consequences of a national government's power to tax under the proposed U.S. Constitution. Focuses on constitutional construction, exclusive vs. concurrent powers, necessity/propriety and supremacy clauses, and practical considerations about revenue and defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary truths / first principles for political reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain primary truths, or first principles, upon which all subsequent reasonings must depend. Examples: 'the whole is greater than its part; things equal to the same are equal to one another; two straight lines cannot enclose a space; and all right angles are equal to each other.' Similar maxims in ethics and politics include: 'there cannot be an effect without a cause; that the means ought to be proportioned to the end; that every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these axiomatic propositions (and their analogues in politics) as the foundational tests for subsequent arguments. Beware of passions, prejudices, and sophistry that obscure these obvious principles. If a conclusion fails to conform to these primary truths, suspect defect in perception or undue bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must possess every power requisite to accomplish entrusted objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A government ought to contain in itself every power requisite to the full accomplishment of the objects committed to its care, and to the complete execution of the trusts for which it is responsible, free from every other control but a regard to the public good and to the sense of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a power should be conferred on a government, ask whether that power is necessary to accomplish the government's assigned objects; if so, the power should reside in that government subject to popular control, not external restraints that thwart its duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends; powers commensurate with objects
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The means ought to be proportioned to the end' and 'every power ought to be commensurate with its object' — powers granted must be sufficient in scope to accomplish their aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificial limits on powers that would render the entrusted ends unattainable. This includes providing capacity to meet future, unforeseen exigencies necessary to the office's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide for national defense/public peace should be bounded only by exigencies and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: As the duties of superintending the national defense and of securing the public peace against foreign or domestic violence involve a provision for casualties and dangers to which no possible limits can be assigned, the power of making that provision ought to know no other bounds than the exigencies of the nation and the resources of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal and legislative capacity relevant to national defense must be adaptable and indefinite enough to respond to unforeseeable future threats; designing constitutions on present exigencies risks leaving the community defenseless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue is the essential engine; power to procure revenue must be included
rubrics_metrics.description: As revenue is the essential engine by which the means of answering the national exigencies must be procured, the power of procuring that article in its full extent must necessarily be comprehended in that of providing for those exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because revenue enables all other national functions, the ability to tax (or otherwise raise revenue) should be vested where responsibility for national exigencies resides; otherwise the government cannot fulfill its duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must have practical (unqualified) power to tax in ordinary modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory and practice conspire to prove that the power of procuring revenue is unavailing when exercised over the States in their collective capacities; the federal government must of necessity be invested with an unqualified power of taxation in the ordinary modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the allocation of taxation powers by considering practical efficacy: collective reliance on separate state governments for federal revenue is inadequate; the national government needs direct, effective taxing powers to raise funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule for exclusive delegation of state sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive delegation of power to the Union exists only in three cases: where the Constitution in express terms granted an exclusive authority to the Union; where it granted in one instance an authority to the Union, and in another prohibited the States from exercising the like authority; and where it granted an authority to the Union to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three-fold tests to determine whether a power is exclusively federal. Examples given: exclusive legislation over the federal district (express grant); duties on imports/exports (grant plus prohibition on states); uniform rule of naturalization (mutual repugnancy if states had distinct rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction for most taxation (states retain taxing powers except specified exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports is manifestly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States. The Constitution's restriction on states taxing imports/exports implies an affirmation that the States retain authority to tax other articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that federal grants necessarily exclude state taxing unless the text or necessary repugnancy requires it; treat taxation over non-import/export articles as concurrent, with practical conflicts to be resolved by prudence and cooperation rather than implied exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative pregnant as an interpretive indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction that 'no State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports' is a 'negative pregnant' — a negation of one thing and an affirmation of another, i.e., a negation of state authority over imports/exports and an implied affirmation of their authority over other taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the Constitution expressly prohibits a specific state exercise, infer that other powers not prohibited were intended to remain with the States; avoid construing prohibitions so as to create absurd or unnecessary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and Proper clause is declaratory; means to execute powers included
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing Congress 'to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution THE POWERS by that Constitution vested' is essentially declaratory: a power to lay and collect taxes must include power to pass laws necessary and proper to execute that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the clause as affirming what necessarily follows from granting a power; focus scrutiny on the specific substantive powers granted rather than on the sweeping declaratory phrase itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy clause limited to acts pursuant to the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The second clause of the sixth article declares that the Constitution and laws made 'IN PURSUANCE THEREOF' shall be the supreme law of the land; supremacy is expressly confined to laws made pursuant to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that laws that are not 'pursuant to' constitutional powers are usurpations and not entitled to supremacy; supremacy does not validate acts beyond the constitutional grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who judges necessity and propriety; remedy for overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must judge in the first instance of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last. If the federal government overpasses its authority, the people must appeal to the standard they have formed and take measures to redress the injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive disputes about necessity/propriety are first for the political branches; ultimate corrective is popular or constitutional remedy rather than abstract disqualification of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate constitutional dangers by government structure, not speculative usurpation fears
rubrics_metrics.description: All observations founded upon the danger of usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers. If the proposed construction affords like species of security as state constitutions, apprehensions of usurpation should be discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anti-usurpation protections (composition, dependence on people, institutional checks) rather than attempting to limit necessary powers on the presumption of future abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design constitutions to provide capacity for future contingencies (not only present needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed upon a calculation of existing exigencies, but upon a combination of these with the probable exigencies of ages. There ought to be a capacity to provide for future contingencies as they may happen; and as these are illimitable in their nature, it is impossible safely to limit that capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allocating powers and financial capacity, account for long-term needs (e.g., defense, naval forces, wars, debts) rather than fixing limits based only on current circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual interest and prudence should prevent injudicious accumulation or interference in concurrent taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Though an improper accumulation of taxes on the same object might render collection difficult or precarious, this would be a mutual inconvenience, not arising from a superiority or defect of power on either side, but from injudicious exercise by one or the other. Mutual interest would dictate concert to avoid material inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve potential conflicts in concurrent taxation through prudence, mutual accommodation, and practical cooperation rather than through implied constitutional exclusivity.
